question: Managed by the EQT Group and funded to the tune of EUR 1 billion by the Commission, the Scaleup Europe Fund (SEF) is a EUR 5 billion partnership that was launched to support highpotential EU companies and therefore encourage ‘the best of Europe to choose Europe’.

However, SEF recently took part in Lovable’s Series C funding round, even though the Swedish company had already transferred its registered office, voting rights, intellectual property and tax base to Delaware in the US. In other words, by deploying resources from Series B onwards, the EU is funding companies that have already relocated.

Another issue is that the SEF’s resources are a drop in the ocean compared to the investments made by US tech giants. In the light of the fact that EU venture capital funds should not finance US companies – and thus undermine Europe’s technological sovereignty, tax base and ability to regulate these companies’ activities – I ask the Commission: 1.
Will it make public fund disbursement conditional on companies maintaining their registered offices and tax bases in the European Union?

What structural changes will it make to the start-up/scaleup strategy so that the EU can invest at an earlier stage and prevent strategic companies from feeling like they have to relocate to the US in order to raise capital?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.10.2026) The Scaleup Europe Fund (SEF) addresses Europe’s growth-capital gap in innovation and supports technological sovereignty by helping high-potential companies scale globally while keeping their European base. At least 80% of the SEF capital should be private.

SEF is set up as a market-standard fund, and an independent investment adviser has been appointed to take investment decisions under a delegated mandate. The fund focuses on companies established in the EU and Horizon Europe eligibility rules apply to the investments in which the EU opts to partake.

The SEF mandate provides a limited flexibility to invest in companies that are not eligible under the Horizon Europe rules. Where such an investment is made, the EU budget is not used, and only private capital is deployed.

Compliance with these limits is required by the portfolio manager and monitored by the Fund’s alternative investment fund manager, by the European Innovation Council Fund Board, and by the Commission. Alongside the SEF, the EU Startup and Scaleup Strategy1 addresses several measures intended to reduce the incentives for startups to incorporate their business or relocate outside the EU.

The strategy addresses the underlying causes: market fragmentation, regulatory complexity, weak exit opportunities, talent bottlenecks, and limited access to infrastructure and customers. The key initiative to prevent companies from incorporating outside the EU is the EU-wide legal framework for companies, EU Inc2.
The aim is to let startups set up, operate, attract investment and expand across the EU under one common regime instead of having to navigate fragmented national rules.
